Chapter 11: The Absurd Creator—Art, Imagination, and the Act of Making.
There’s something quietly rebellious about the moment someone decides to create. Picture a painter, alone in their studio, swirling colors into shapes that only they can imagine. Or a writer, tapping away into the night, chasing down a feeling that just won’t sit still.
Creation isn’t about solving the absurd or making it disappear. Instead, it’s about giving that chaos some sort of shape—turning it into something we can see, touch, or even share.
You might not see yourself as an artist, but honestly, everyone creates in their own way. Think about a meal you’ve cooked with real care, or a story you told just to make a child smile. Maybe it’s planting a little garden in a forgotten corner of your yard. Each of these things is an act of making—of bringing something new into the world where there was nothing before.
The absurd creator doesn’t wait for permission or applause. They understand their work might never be finished, or fully understood, or even noticed at all. But they keep creating anyway, because just doing the work—just making—is meaningful all on its own.
And here’s where it gets interesting: there’s a real freedom in this kind of making. When you create, you become the author of your own story. You shape your world, even if it’s in small, quiet ways. That’s how we claim our humanity. The absurd might always be there in the background, but suddenly, it isn’t so overwhelming. It loses a little of its sting.
For some folks, creating helps make sense of things. For others, it’s a way to push back against the darkness—a source of pure joy in the doing. The world might not care, but our creations do. They’re acts of hope and courage, little sparks of love sent out into the unknown.
So, as the day winds down and everything grows quiet, the absurd creator is still at it. The struggle goes on—not as something heavy, but as a way of truly living. It’s a simple, defiant way of saying yes to life, even if we never get all the answers.
